steps.title: Filter Records
steps.description: Decide whether to retain or exclude records flagged as potentially problematic based on missingness patterns or extreme outlier values in key covariates.

options.label: Keep All Records
options.rationale: Retain full sample to maximize power and avoid selection bias; missingness handled via model specification.
options.spec: Return the input DataFrame unchanged; no rows dropped.

options.label: Exclude Extreme Outliers in Balance, Duration, Campaign, Previous
options.rationale: Remove observations with extreme values in balance, duration, campaign, or previous that may unduly influence logistic regression estimates due to leverage or model misspecification.
options.spec: Drop rows where balance < -5000 or balance > 80000 or duration > 3000 or campaign > 30 or previous > 50; return filtered DataFrame.

steps.title: Handle Missing Values
steps.description: Choose how to address missing values in categorical predictors (job, education, contact, poutcome) which are common and may bias complete-case analysis.

options.label: Treat Missing as Separate Category
options.rationale: Preserve sample size and avoid assumptions about missingness by explicitly modeling missingness as a meaningful category (e.g., 'unknown').
options.spec: For each of job, education, contact, poutcome: fill NaN with 'missing'; return DataFrame with these columns updated; no new columns created.

options.label: Mode Impute and Add Missingness Indicators
options.rationale: Impute missing values with mode to allow use in models requiring complete data, while retaining information about which values were imputed via binary flags.
options.spec: For each of job, education, contact, poutcome: compute mode; fill NaN with mode; create new binary column {col}_was_missing (1 if originally NaN, else 0); return DataFrame with imputed columns and four new flag columns.

options.label: Drop Rows with Any Missing in Covariates
options.rationale: Ensure clean data for model fitting by removing ambiguity; acceptable if missingness is low and MCAR, though here it is not negligible.
options.spec: Drop rows where any of job, education, contact, poutcome is NaN; return filtered DataFrame.

steps.title: Encode Categorical Features
steps.description: Select encoding method for multinomial categorical variables (job, marital, education, default, housing, loan, contact, month, poutcome) to represent them in logistic regression.

options.label: One-Hot Encoding with Reference Level Dropped
options.rationale: Standard approach to avoid perfect multicollinearity; each category compared to a reference level; coefficients interpretable as log-odds vs reference.
options.spec: For each categorical column in ['job', 'marital', 'education', 'default', 'housing', 'loan', 'contact', 'month', 'poutcome']: create dummy variables, drop first category; return DataFrame with original columns replaced by their dummy variants (e.g., job_management, job_technician, etc.).

options.label: One-Hot Encoding with All Levels Kept
options.rationale: Useful in regularized models or when avoiding arbitrary reference choice; though causes collinearity, some software handles it; here we interpret via effects or drop intercept.
options.spec: For each categorical column in ['job', 'marital', 'education', 'default', 'housing', 'loan', 'contact', 'month', 'poutcome']: create dummy variables for all categories; return DataFrame with original columns replaced by full set of dummies.

options.label: Ordinal Encoding for Education (Assuming Order)
options.rationale: Education has natural ordering (primary < secondary < tertiary); encoding as ordinal preserves order and reduces dimensionality; assume proportional effect per level increase.
options.spec: Map education: 'primary' -> 0, 'secondary' -> 1, 'tertiary' -> 2; fill missing with 1 (mode); return DataFrame with 'education_ord' replacing 'education'.

options.code:
import pandas as pd

def apply(df, ctx):
    cols = ['job', 'marital', 'education', 'default', 'housing', 'loan', 'contact', 'month', 'poutcome']
    for col in cols:
        dummies = pd.get_dummies(df[col], prefix=col, prefix_sep='_', dtype=int)
        df = pd.concat([df, dummies], axis=1)
    return df

options.rationale: Default maximum likelihood estimation with standard errors from inverse Hessian; assumes correct model specification and independent observations.
options.spec: Fit statsmodels.Logit(y, X) where X includes campaign (as linear term) and all features produced by prior steps; add intercept; extract coefficient for campaign, exponentiate for OR; compute Wald 95% CI and p-value; return dict with keys: estimate (OR), ci_low, ci_high, p_value.
options.code:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import statsmodels.api as sm
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

def estimate(df, ctx):
    # Use only complete cases for modeling
    cols_used = ['y', 'campaign'] + list(df.columns)
    data = df.dropna(subset=cols_used)
    n = len(data)
    if n == 0:
        return {"estimate": 0.0, "ci_low": 0.0, "ci_high": 0.0, "p_value": 1.0, "n": 0}
    # Fit logistic regression with campaign as linear term
    model = sm.Logit(data['y'], sm.add_constant(data['campaign'])).fit(disp=False)
    coef = model.params['campaign']
    or_ = np.exp(coef)
    ci_low, ci_high = model.conf_int().loc['campaign']
    ci_low, ci_high = np.exp([ci_low, ci_high])
    p_val = model.pvalues['campaign']
    return {"estimate": float(or_), "ci_low": float(ci_low), "ci_high": float(ci_high), "p_value": float(p_val), "n": int(n)}

options.rationale: Protect against misspecification of error distribution or mild dependence; SEs consistent under weaker assumptions; widely recommended for inference.
options.spec: Fit statsmodels.Logit(y, X) with same X as above; use cov_type='HC0' to get robust covariance matrix; extract campaign coefficient, exponentiate for OR; compute 95% CI and p-value using robust SE; return dict with estimate, ci_low, ci_high, p_value.

option.label: Exclude Customers With Very High Contact Frequency And Prior Outreach
option.rationale: Removing extreme values in campaign and previous may reduce bias from highly engaged or resistant customers, potentially weakening the observed negative association.
option.spec: Drop rows where campaign > 20 or previous > 20; return filtered DataFrame.

option.label: Impute Missing Values With Mode
option.rationale: Replacing missing categorical values with the mode may alter the distribution of covariates in a way that attenuates the estimated effect of campaign calls.
option.spec: For each of job, education, contact, poutcome: fill NaN with the most frequent non-missing value in that column; return DataFrame with these columns updated; no new columns created.

option.label: Firth Penalized Logistic Regression
option.rationale: Firth regression reduces small-sample bias in logistic regression; though sample size is large, it may shrink the campaign coefficient toward null, increasing the OR toward or above 1.
option.spec: Use statsmodels.Logit with method='bfgs' and start_params initialized to zero, adding a Jeffreys prior-like penalty via manual log-likelihood adjustment (or use logistf if available); exponentiate campaign coefficient for OR; compute profile likelihood CI and p-value; return dict with estimate, ci_low, ci_high, p_value.

option.label: Add Quadratic Term For Campaign To Capture Nonlinearity
option.rationale: The true relationship may be nonlinear; adding a squared term could reveal that the marginal effect diminishes or reverses at higher values, and the linear term alone may overstate the negative effect.
option.spec: Create a new column campaign_squared = campaign ** 2; include both campaign and campaign_squared in X; extract coefficient for campaign, exponentiate for OR (interpreted as marginal effect at zero); compute Wald 95% CI and p-value; return dict with estimate, ci_low, ci_high, p_value.

data.reason: Excluding outliers based on arbitrary thresholds (>20 calls) risks selection bias by removing informative extremes without justification tied to data distribution or measurement error, potentially distorting the exposure-outcome relationship.

Firth logistic regression addresses small-sample bias but is unnecessary here given large sample size; its shrinkage toward null introduces bias away from the true effect without clear justification, potentially altering interpretation.

Imputing missing categorical data with the mode distorts the true distribution by over-representing the most frequent category, potentially biasing estimates—especially if missingness is informative—and lacks strong justification without evidence MCAR.

Adding a quadratic term without centering makes the linear coefficient represent the effect at campaign=0, which is often outside the data range and hard to interpret; moreover, the estimand is defined as the odds ratio per additional contact call assuming a linear log-odds relationship, so introducing nonlinearity changes the estimand unless the marginal effect is averaged or evaluated at a meaningful value.

    mask = (~df['job'].isna()) & (~df['education'].isna()) & (~df['contact'].isna()) & (~df['poutcome'].isna())
    return df[mask].copy()

options.code:
import pandas as pd

def apply(df, ctx):
    cols = ['job', 'marital', 'education', 'default', 'housing', 'loan', 'contact', 'month', 'poutcome']
    for col in cols:
        dummies = pd.get_dummies(df[col], prefix=col, prefix_sep='_', dtype=int)
        df = pd.concat([df, dummies], axis=1)
    return df

options.spec: Fit statsmodels.Logit(y, X) where X includes campaign (as linear term) and all features produced by prior steps; add intercept; extract coefficient for campaign, exponentiate for OR; compute Wald 95% CI and p-value; return dict with keys: estimate (OR), ci_low, ci_high, p_value.
options.code:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import statsmodels.api as sm
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

def estimate(df, ctx):
    # Use only complete cases for modeling
    cols_used = ['y', 'campaign'] + list(df.columns)
    data = df.dropna(subset=cols_used)
    n = len(data)
    if n == 0:
        return {"estimate": 0.0, "ci_low": 0.0, "ci_high": 0.0, "p_value": 1.0, "n": 0}
    # Fit logistic regression with campaign as linear term
    model = sm.Logit(data['y'], sm.add_constant(data['campaign'])).fit(disp=False)
    coef = model.params['campaign']
    or_ = np.exp(coef)
    ci_low, ci_high = model.conf_int().loc['campaign']
    ci_low, ci_high = np.exp([ci_low, ci_high])
    p_val = model.pvalues['campaign']
    return {"estimate": float(or_), "ci_low": float(ci_low), "ci_high": float(ci_high), "p_value": float(p_val), "n": int(n)}

options.label: Logistic Regression with Huber-White Robust SE
options.rationale: Protect against misspecification of error distribution or mild dependence; SEs consistent under weaker assumptions; widely recommended for inference.
options.spec: Fit statsmodels.Logit(y, X) with same X as above; use cov_type='HC0' to get robust covariance matrix; extract campaign coefficient, exponentiate for OR; compute 95% CI and p-value using robust SE; return dict with estimate, ci_low, ci_high, p_value.

report.question: Does each additional contact call to the same customer in a campaign reduce the chance that the customer subscribes to a term deposit?

changes.to_label: Drop Rows with Any Missing in Covariates
changes.rationale: Ensure clean data for model fitting by removing ambiguity; acceptable if missingness is low and MCAR, though here it is not negligible.

changes.to_label: Logistic Regression with Huber-White Robust SE
changes.rationale: Protect against misspecification of error distribution or mild dependence; SEs consistent under weaker assumptions; widely recommended for inference.

report.narrative: The original analysis found that each additional contact call reduces the odds of subscribing to a term deposit (odds ratio = 0.88, 95% CI [0.86, 0.89], p < 0.001), supporting a verdict to CAP THE CALLS. A minimal flip was identified requiring two defensible changes: (1) dropping rows with any missing covariates instead of treating missingness as a category, which is acceptable if missingness is low and missing completely at random, though here it is not negligible; and (2) using logistic regression with Huber-White robust standard errors instead of standard logistic regression, which protects against misspecification of the error distribution or mild dependence and is widely recommended for inference. Together, these changes increased the sample size reduction (from 45,211 to 7,842 observations) and widened the confidence interval to [0.61, 1.27], yielding a non-significant p-value of 0.50 and flipping the verdict to NO CASE FOR A CAP. This flip was reproduced by an independent re-execution. Across 7 explored analytical universes, 85.7% agreed with the original verdict, indicating moderate robustness.
caveats: The flipped result relies on a substantially reduced sample (7,842 vs 45,211), which may introduce selection bias if missingness is not completely at random.
Robustness (85.7%) reflects agreement across only 7 explored universes; a broader search might yield different proportions.
Influence figures describe sensitivity to analyst choices, not causal effects in the world.
The minimal flip combines two changes; the individual contribution of each change to the verdict reversal is not isolated.
